newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian MPS told not to clap Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Australian MPS told not to clap Clinton.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton has yet to make his historic addresss to a joint sitting of Australia's parliament, but already protocol-preoccupied politicians are pondering whether he should receive a standing ovation and just where, and how high, he'll sit.

Government backbencher John Southcott asked House of Representatives speaker Bob Halverson if a standing ovation would be okay, "subject to members' and senators' inclination" after Clinton's speech on Wednesday.
Haverson at first thought that would be fitting, until he received a gentle reminder from Prime Minister John Howard.
"The prime minister has just reminded me that it is unparliamentary for members to clap," he told parliament.
"The conventional way of supporting those initiatives that we hear in the chamber is by the traditional 'hear, hear!'."
And, he sternly warned: "I ask members to desist forthwith from what is a very poor practice of beating their desks."
Clinton will sit at Halverson's right, "on a podium that is raised six or seven inches (15-17.5 centimetres) from the ground".
And where will he make the speech?
"We have looked at this very carefully and indeed have decided that the president will address us from directly in front of me," said Halverson, who sits at the front-centre of the chamber.

Clinton is due to address a joint meeting of the upper house Senate and the House of Representatives on Wednesday, becoming only the second U.S. president to make such an address after George Bush in 1991.
